claim: Head and neck cancer is among the ten most common cancers in Europe, with an age standardised incidence rate of 10.3 per 100,000 person-years.
source: Head and neck cancer (HNC) is among the ten most common cancers in Europe, with an age standardised incidence rate of 10.3 per 100,000 person-years (Global cancer observatory: cancer today, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the Global cancer observatory: cancer today, 2022.

claim: Around 90% of head and neck cancers are classed as squamous cell carcinomas of the oral cavity, pharynx, or larynx.
source: Around 90% of HNCs are classed as squamous cell carcinomas of the oral cavity, pharynx, or larynx (Curado and Hashibe, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Curado and Hashibe, 2009.

claim: Tobacco smoking and alcohol consumption are well-established head and neck cancer risk factors.
source: Tobacco smoking and alcohol consumption are well-established HNC risk factors (Hashibe et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2008; Purdue et al., 2009; Hashibe et al., 2009; Marron et al., 2010; IARC Working Group on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, 2004; Gormley et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: High-risk human papillomavirus infection has been causally linked to the risk of head and neck cancer, especially oropharyngeal cancer.
source: High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection has also been causally linked to the risk of HNC, especially oropharyngeal cancer (Sabatini and Chiocca, 2020; Gillison et al., 2000; de Martel et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sabatini and Chiocca, 2020; Gillison et al., 2000; de Martel et al., 2020.

claim: The World Cancer Research Fund/American Institute for Cancer Research Continuous Update Project Expert Report published in 2018 determined higher body fatness likely increases the risk of head and neck cancer.
source: The World Cancer Research Fund/American Institute for Cancer Research (WCRF/AICR) Continuous Update Project (CUP) Expert Report published in 2018 determined higher body fatness (i.e. body mass index [BMI], waist-to-hip ratio [WHR], and waist circumference) likely increases the risk of HNC (World Cancer Research Fund/American Institute for Cancer Research, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Cancer Research Fund/American Institute for Cancer Research, 2018 report.

claim: A higher body mass index has been associated with a decreased risk of head and neck cancer.
source: The CUP panel reached this conclusion even though a higher BMI has been associated with a decreased risk of HNC (World Cancer Research Fund/American Institute for Cancer Research, 2018), since they noted the inverse association appears to be limited to current smokers.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Cancer Research Fund/American Institute for Cancer Research, 2018 report.

claim: The inverse association between body mass index and head and neck cancer risk appears to be limited to current smokers.
source: The CUP panel reached this conclusion even though a higher BMI has been associated with a decreased risk of HNC (World Cancer Research Fund/American Institute for Cancer Research, 2018), since they noted the inverse association appears to be limited to current smokers.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Cancer Research Fund/American Institute for Cancer Research, 2018 report.

claim: Nicotine consumption could lead to appetite suppression and increased energy expenditure, which could in turn lead to weight loss among smokers.
source: It is thought that nicotine consumption could lead to appetite suppression and increased energy expenditure, which could in turn lead to weight loss (and spurious inverse associations between BMI and HNC risk [Gaudet et al., 2015]) among smokers (Jo et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gaudet et al., 2015 and Jo et al., 2002.

claim: Among never smokers, body mass index has been positively associated with head and neck cancer risk.
source: Among never smokers, BMI has been positively associated with HNC risk, in line with the evidence observed for measures of central adiposity (i.e. WHR and waist circumference; Gaudet et al., 2015; Watts et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gaudet et al., 2015 and Watts et al., 2024.

claim: Evidence from Mendelian randomization studies suggests higher adiposity increases the risk of smoking.
source: However, the relationship between adiposity and smoking is complex, with evidence from Mendelian randomization (MR) studies suggesting higher adiposity increases the risk of smoking (Taylor et al., 2019; Carreras-Torres et al., 2018) while simultaneously suggesting smoking may lead to lower adiposity (Taylor et al., 2019; Åsvold et al., 2014; Freathy et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2014; Morris et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Taylor et al., 2019 and Carreras-Torres et al., 2018.

claim: Evidence from Mendelian randomization studies suggests smoking may lead to lower adiposity.
source: However, the relationship between adiposity and smoking is complex, with evidence from Mendelian randomization (MR) studies suggesting higher adiposity increases the risk of smoking (Taylor et al., 2019; Carreras-Torres et al., 2018) while simultaneously suggesting smoking may lead to lower adiposity (Taylor et al., 2019; Åsvold et al., 2014; Freathy et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2014; Morris et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Taylor et al., 2019; Åsvold et al., 2014; Freathy et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2014; Morris et al., 2015.

claim: Excess adiposity, socioeconomic deprivation and smoking are often strongly correlated.
source: Additionally, excess adiposity, socioeconomic deprivation and (both active and passive) smoking are often strongly correlated (Yang et al., 2008; Marmot and Bell, 2019; Marmot, 2017; Filippidis et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2008; Marmot and Bell, 2019; Marmot, 2017; Filippidis et al., 2016.

claim: Previous Mendelian randomization studies on adiposity and head and neck cancer risk were relatively small with a maximum of 6034 cases.
source: It is important to acknowledge that previous MR studies on adiposity (i.e. BMI, WHR, waist circumference) and HNC risk were relatively small (maximum N=6034 cases) and could not fully discount causality due to limited statistical power (Larsson and Burgess, 2021; Gormley et al., 2023; Vithayathil et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Larsson and Burgess, 2021; Gormley et al., 2023; Vithayathil et al., 2021.

claim: Previous Mendelian randomization studies on adiposity and head and neck cancer risk could not fully discount causality due to limited statistical power.
source: It is important to acknowledge that previous MR studies on adiposity (i.e. BMI, WHR, waist circumference) and HNC risk were relatively small (maximum N=6034 cases) and could not fully discount causality due to limited statistical power (Larsson and Burgess, 2021; Gormley et al., 2023; Vithayathil et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Larsson and Burgess, 2021; Gormley et al., 2023; Vithayathil et al., 2021.

claim: The HEADSpAcE consortium GWAS includes over two times the number of cases than the GAME-ON GWAS used by Gormley et al., 2023.
source: Therefore, the aim of this MR study was to revisit the link between adiposity and HNC risk using data from a HNC genome-wide association study (GWAS) that includes over two times the number of cases than the Genetic Associations and Mechanisms in Oncology (GAME-ON) GWAS Lesseur et al., 2016 used by Gormley et al., 2023 (the largest to date; N=12,619, including 6034 cases and 6585 controls) and has more granular data on HNC subsites (i.e. oral cavity, hypopharynx, oropharynx, and larynx).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lesseur et al., 2016 and Gormley et al., 2023, and by inference from the stated sample sizes.

claim: GWAS summary statistics for head and neck cancer were obtained from a European HEADSpAcE consortium GWAS that excluded UK Biobank participants (N=31,523, including 12,264 cases and 19,259 controls).
source: GWAS summary statistics for HNC were obtained from a European HEADSpAcE consortium GWAS that excluded UK Biobank participants (N=31,523, including 12,264 cases and 19,259 controls) to avoid overlapping samples across the exposure and outcome datasets.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript text describing the data source.

claim: The HEADSpAcE GWAS includes the European GAME-ON data used by Lesseur et al., 2016.
source: It includes the European GAME-ON data used by Lesseur et al., 2016 and has more granular data on HNC subsites (i.e. oral cavity [N=21,269, including 3091 cases and 18,178 controls], hypopharynx [N=18,652, including 474 cases and 18,178 controls], HPV positive oropharynx [N=20,146, including 1980 cases and 18,166 controls], HPV negative oropharynx [N=19,114, including 948 cases and 18,166 controls] and larynx [N=20,668, including 2490 cases and 18,178 controls]; Ebrahimi et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lesseur et al., 2016 and Ebrahimi et al., 2024.

claim: After data harmonisation and the removal of ambiguous palindromic SNPs, 442 genetic variants remained as instruments for BMI.
source: After data harmonisation and the removal of ambiguous palindromic SNPs, 442 genetic variants remained as instruments for BMI, while 267 remained for WHR and 353 for waist circumference (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: 267 genetic variants remained as instruments for waist-to-hip ratio after data harmonisation and the removal of ambiguous palindromic SNPs.
source: After data harmonisation and the removal of ambiguous palindromic SNPs, 442 genetic variants remained as instruments for BMI, while 267 remained for WHR and 353 for waist circumference (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: 353 genetic variants remained as instruments for waist circumference after data harmonisation and the removal of ambiguous palindromic SNPs.
source: After data harmonisation and the removal of ambiguous palindromic SNPs, 442 genetic variants remained as instruments for BMI, while 267 remained for WHR and 353 for waist circumference (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: The mean F-statistic for BMI genetic instruments was 77 (range 33–844) and the total variance explained was 4.8%.
source: The mean F-statistic for BMI was 77 (range 33–844) and the total variance explained was 4.8%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: For waist-to-hip ratio, the mean F-statistic was 73 (range 33–820) and the total variance explained was 3.1%.
source: For WHR, the mean F-statistic was 73 (range 33–820) and the total variance explained was 3.1%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: For waist circumference, the mean F-statistic was 58 (range 30–940) and the total variance explained was 4.4%.
source: For waist circumference, the mean F-statistic was 58 (range 30–940) and the total variance explained was 4.4%.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Using the BMI genetic instruments (total R2=4.8%) and an α of 0.05, the study had 80% statistical power to detect an OR as small as 1.16 for head and neck cancer risk.
source: Using the BMI genetic instruments (total R2=4.8%) and an α of 0.05, we had 80% statistical power to detect an OR as small as 1.16 for HNC risk (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: For waist-to-hip ratio (total R2=3.1%), the study could detect odds ratios as small as 1.20.
source: For WHR (total R2=3.1%) and waist circumference (total R2=4.4%), we could detect odds ratios (ORs) as small as 1.20 and 1.17, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: For waist circumference (total R2=4.4%), the study could detect odds ratios as small as 1.17.
source: For WHR (total R2=3.1%) and waist circumference (total R2=4.4%), we could detect odds ratios (ORs) as small as 1.20 and 1.17, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In univariable MR, higher genetically predicted BMI increased the risk of overall head and neck cancer (IVW OR = 1.17 per 1-SD higher BMI, 95% CI 1.02–1.34, p=0.03).
source: In univariable MR, higher genetically predicted BMI increased the risk of overall HNC (IVW OR = 1.17 per 1 standard deviation [1-SD] higher BMI, 95% CI 1.02–1.34, p=0.03), with no heterogeneity across subsites (Q p=0.78; Figure 2, Appendix 1—figure 3 and Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text and referenced in Figure 2, Appendix 1—figure 3 and Supplementary file 1G.

claim: There was no heterogeneity across subsites for the effect of BMI on head and neck cancer risk (Q p=0.78).
source: In univariable MR, higher genetically predicted BMI increased the risk of overall HNC (IVW OR = 1.17 per 1 standard deviation [1-SD] higher BMI, 95% CI 1.02–1.34, p=0.03), with no heterogeneity across subsites (Q p=0.78; Figure 2, Appendix 1—figure 3 and Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text.

claim: The positive relationship between genetically predicted BMI and head and neck cancer risk was not consistent across the MR-Egger, weighted median and weighted mode analyses.
source: However, the positive relationship between genetically predicted BMI and HNC risk was not consistent across the MR-Egger, weighted median and weighted mode analyses, with point estimates in opposing directions and confidence intervals including the null.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text.

claim: The Q statistic test suggested that there was heterogeneity across individual SNP estimates for BMI and head and neck cancer (Q=609, p<0.001).
source: The Q statistic and MR-Egger intercept tests suggested that there was heterogeneity across individual SNP estimates (Q=609, p<0.001) and a minor degree of unbalanced horizontal pleiotropy (intercept = 0.007, p=0.03) that could have biased the main IVW results (Supplementary file 1H and Supplementary file 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text and referenced in Supplementary file 1H and Supplementary file 1I.

claim: The MR-Egger intercept test suggested a minor degree of unbalanced horizontal pleiotropy (intercept = 0.007, p=0.03) that could have biased the main IVW results for BMI and head and neck cancer.

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text and referenced in Supplementary file 1H and Supplementary file 1I.

claim: The MR-PRESSO analysis identified two outliers (rs11611246 and rs9603697) for BMI and head and neck cancer.
source: Although the MR-PRESSO analysis identified two outliers (i.e. rs11611246 and rs9603697), the distortion test suggested the outlier-corrected estimate (outlier-corrected IVW OR = 1.14 per 1-SD higher BMI, 95% CI 1.00–1.30, p=0.05) was not statistically different to the main IVW estimate (p=0.94; Supplementary file 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text and referenced in Supplementary file 1J.

source: In univariable IVW MR, both CSI and SI were linked to an increased risk of HNC (CSI OR = 4.47 per 1-SD higher CSI, 95% CI 3.31–6.03, p<0.001; SI OR = 2.07 per 1-SD higher SI 95% CI 1.60–2.68, p<0.001; note in Supplementary file 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text and referenced in Supplementary file 1K.

claim: In univariable IVW MR, smoking initiation was linked to an increased risk of head and neck cancer (SI OR = 2.07 per 1-SD higher SI 95% CI 1.60–2.68, p<0.001).

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text and referenced in Supplementary file 1K.

claim: The effect of BMI on head and neck cancer risk was attenuated when smoking behaviour was included in the MVMR model (OR accounting for CSI = 0.93 per 1-SD higher BMI, 95% CI 0.78–1.12, p=0.47).
source: The effect of BMI on HNC risk was attenuated when smoking behaviour was included in the MVMR model (OR accounting for CSI = 0.93 per 1-SD higher BMI, 95% CI 0.78–1.12, p=0.47; OR accounting for smoking initiation = 1.09 per 1-SD higher BMI, 95% CI 0.88–1.34, p=0.43; Figures 5 and 6 and Supplementary file 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text and referenced in Figures 5 and 6 and Supplementary file 1K.

claim: The effect of BMI on head and neck cancer risk was attenuated when smoking initiation was included in the MVMR model (OR accounting for smoking initiation = 1.09 per 1-SD higher BMI, 95% CI 0.88–1.34, p=0.43).

claim: After removing six SNPs (rs10002111, rs2503185, rs264941, rs10858334, rs225882, rs2273175) that were more strongly associated with smoking behaviour than BMI, the genetically predicted effect of BMI on head and neck cancer risk slightly attenuated towards the null (Steiger filtered IVW OR = 1.14 per 1-SD higher BMI, 95% CI 1.00–1.31, p=0.05).

claim: The CAUSE analysis did not find evidence against bias due to correlated pleiotropy, since the causal model did not fit the data much better than the sharing model (CAUSE OR 1.12 per 1-SD higher BMI, 95% credible interval 0.93–1.34, delta ELPD for sharing vs causal = −0.07, p=0.47).

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text and referenced in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: Neither the sharing nor the causal model fitted the data much better than the null model in the CAUSE analysis (delta ELPD for null vs sharing = −0.39, p=0.36; and delta ELPD for null vs causal = −0.46, p=0.41).
source: Interestingly, neither the sharing nor the causal model fitted the data much better than the null model (delta ELPD for null vs sharing = −0.39, p=0.36; and delta ELPD for null vs causal = −0.46, p=0.41).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text.

claim: After filtering SNPs with conditional probabilities <0.8 and clusters with fewer than four SNPs, only a null cluster including 372 SNPs (424 before filtering) remained in the MR-Clust output for BMI and head and neck cancer risk.
source: After filtering SNPs with conditional probabilities <0.8 and clusters with fewer than four SNPs (e.g. cluster 1, as only three of 17 SNPs remained after probability filtering), only a null cluster including 372 SNPs (424 before filtering) remained in the MR-Clust output for BMI and HNC risk (Appendix 1—figure 7 and Supplementary file 1M).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text and referenced in Appendix 1—figure 7 and Supplementary file 1M.

claim: The MR-Clust analysis did not reveal any mechanistic pathways underlying the effect observed between BMI and head and neck cancer risk.
source: Hence, the MR-Clust analysis did not reveal any mechanistic pathways underlying the effect observed.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the MR-Clust results showing only a null cluster.

claim: The study did not find consistent evidence of genetically predicted effects of other anthropometric measures on head and neck cancer risk.

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text and referenced in multiple appendix figures and Supplementary file 1N.

claim: The IVW estimate for PC2 capturing a combination of taller height and slimmer waist suggested this body shape decreased head and neck cancer risk (OR = 0.86, 95% CI 0.75–0.99, p=0.04).
source: The IVW estimate for PC2 capturing a combination of taller height and slimmer waist suggested this body shape decreased HNC risk (OR = 0.86, 95% CI 0.75–0.99, p=0.04; Appendix 1—figure 8b).

claim: The IVW estimate for PC3 capturing a combination of taller height and narrower hips suggested this body shape reduced head and neck cancer risk (OR = 0.73, 95% CI 0.55–0.97, p=0.03).
source: Similarly, the IVW estimate for PC3 capturing a combination of taller height and narrower hips suggested this body shape also reduced HNC risk (OR = 0.73, 95% CI 0.55–0.97, p=0.03; Appendix 1—figure 8c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text and referenced in Appendix 1—figure 8c.

claim: The inverse relationships between PC2 and PC3 body shapes and head and neck cancer risk were not consistent with results obtained using pleiotropy-robust methods (MR-Egger, weighted median, and weighted mode).
source: However, these inverse relationships were not consistent with results obtained using pleiotropy-robust methods (i.e. MR-Egger, weighted median, and weighted mode).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text.

claim: Previous MR studies suggest adiposity does not influence head and neck cancer risk.
source: Previous MR studies suggest adiposity does not influence HNC risk (Larsson and Burgess, 2021; Gormley et al., 2023; Vithayathil et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Larsson and Burgess, 2021; Gormley et al., 2023; Vithayathil et al., 2021.

claim: Gormley et al., 2023 did not find a genetically predicted effect of BMI on combined oral and oropharyngeal cancer (OR = 0.89 per 1-SD, 95% CI 0.72–1.09, p=0.26).
source: Gormley et al., 2023 did not find a genetically predicted effect of adiposity on combined oral and oropharyngeal cancer when investigating either BMI (OR = 0.89 per 1-SD, 95% CI 0.72–1.09, p=0.26), WHR (OR = 0.98 per 1-SD, 95% CI 0.74–1.29, p=0.88) or waist circumference (OR = 0.73 per 1-SD, 95% CI 0.52–1.02, p=0.07) as risk factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gormley et al., 2023.

claim: Gormley et al., 2023 did not find a genetically predicted effect of waist-to-hip ratio on combined oral and oropharyngeal cancer (OR = 0.98 per 1-SD, 95% CI 0.74–1.29, p=0.88).
source: Gormley et al., 2023 did not find a genetically predicted effect of adiposity on combined oral and oropharyngeal cancer when investigating either BMI (OR = 0.89 per 1-SD, 95% CI 0.72–1.09, p=0.26), WHR (OR = 0.98 per 1-SD, 95% CI 0.74–1.29, p=0.88) or waist circumference (OR = 0.73 per 1-SD, 95% CI 0.52–1.02, p=0.07) as risk factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gormley et al., 2023.

claim: Gormley et al., 2023 did not find a genetically predicted effect of waist circumference on combined oral and oropharyngeal cancer (OR = 0.73 per 1-SD, 95% CI 0.52–1.02, p=0.07).
source: Gormley et al., 2023 did not find a genetically predicted effect of adiposity on combined oral and oropharyngeal cancer when investigating either BMI (OR = 0.89 per 1-SD, 95% CI 0.72–1.09, p=0.26), WHR (OR = 0.98 per 1-SD, 95% CI 0.74–1.29, p=0.88) or waist circumference (OR = 0.73 per 1-SD, 95% CI 0.52–1.02, p=0.07) as risk factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gormley et al., 2023.

claim: Vithayathil et al., 2021 found no link between BMI and head and neck cancer risk in a study including 367,561 UK Biobank participants (of which 1983 were HNC cases) (OR = 0.98 per 1-SD higher BMI, 95% CI 0.93–1.02, p=0.35).
source: Similarly, a large two-sample MR study by Vithayathil et al., 2021 including 367,561 UK Biobank participants (of which 1983 were HNC cases) found no link between BMI and HNC risk (OR = 0.98 per 1-SD higher BMI, 95% CI 0.93–1.02, p=0.35).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vithayathil et al., 2021.

claim: Larsson and Burgess, 2021 meta-analysed Vithayathil et al., 2021 findings with results obtained using FinnGen data to increase the sample size (N=586,353, including 2109 cases), but still did not find a genetically predicted effect of BMI on head and neck cancer risk (OR = 0.96 per 1-SD higher BMI, 95% CI 0.77–1.19, p=0.69).
source: Larsson and Burgess, 2021 meta-analysed Vithayathil et al., 2021 findings with results obtained using FinnGen data to increase the sample size even further (N=586,353, including 2109 cases), but still did not find a genetically predicted effect of BMI on HNC risk (OR = 0.96 per 1-SD higher BMI, 95% CI 0.77–1.19, p=0.69).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Larsson and Burgess, 2021 and Vithayathil et al., 2021.

claim: The study found some evidence that the genetically predicted effect of BMI on head and neck cancer risk was influenced by smoking.
source: In our study, we found some evidence that the genetically predicted effect of BMI on HNC risk was influenced by smoking.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text.

claim: The genetically predicted effect of BMI on head and neck cancer risk being influenced by smoking could be due to the bidirectional relationship between smoking and adiposity reported in previous MR studies.
source: This could be due to the bidirectional relationship between smoking and adiposity reported in previous MR studies (Taylor et al., 2019; Carreras-Torres et al., 2018; Åsvold et al., 2014; Freathy et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2014; Morris et al., 2015) or due to their shared genetic architecture (Thorgeirsson et al., 2013; Wills and Hopfer, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies and represents speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The genetically predicted effect of BMI on head and neck cancer risk being influenced by smoking could be due to the shared genetic architecture between smoking and adiposity.
source: This could be due to the bidirectional relationship between smoking and adiposity reported in previous MR studies (Taylor et al., 2019; Carreras-Torres et al., 2018; Åsvold et al., 2014; Freathy et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2014; Morris et al., 2015) or due to their shared genetic architecture (Thorgeirsson et al., 2013; Wills and Hopfer, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thorgeirsson et al., 2013 and Wills and Hopfer, 2019 and represents speculation about the mechanism.

claim: This study was the first to exploit multivariable Mendelian randomization to disentangle the effects of BMI and smoking behaviour on the risk of head and neck cancer and its subsites.
source: A strength of our study was that it was the first to exploit MVMR to disentangle the effects of BMI and smoking behaviour on the risk of HNC and its subsites.
evidence: The claim is supported by the manuscript text describing the novelty of the approach.

claim: Some of the SNPs used to instrument smoking behaviour traits have been associated with risk-taking phenotypes and socioeconomic factors.
source: Yet, we acknowledge the smoking behaviour traits used in our MVMR analyses likely capture more than just smoking, since some of the SNPs used to instrument these traits have been associated with risk-taking phenotypes and socioeconomic factors (Gage et al., 2022; Schellhas et al., 2021; Khouja et al., 2021; Reed et al., 2025).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gage et al., 2022; Schellhas et al., 2021; Khouja et al., 2021; Reed et al., 2025.

claim: The HEADSpAcE consortium GWAS used had a large sample size which conferred more statistical power to detect effects of adiposity on head and neck cancer risk compared to previous MR analyses.
source: An important strength of our study was that the HEADSpAcE consortium GWAS used had a large sample size which conferred more statistical power to detect effects of adiposity on HNC risk compared to previous MR analyses (Larsson and Burgess, 2021; Gormley et al., 2023; Vithayathil et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and by inference from the larger sample size.

claim: The availability of data on more head and neck cancer subsites, including oropharyngeal cancers by HPV status, allowed the study to investigate the relationship between adiposity and head and neck cancer risk in more detail than previous MR studies.
source: Furthermore, the availability of data on more HNC subsites, including oropharyngeal cancers by HPV status, allowed us to investigate the relationship between adiposity and HNC risk in more detail than previous MR studies which limited their subsite analyses to oral cavity and overall oropharyngeal cancers (Gormley et al., 2023; Gui et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gormley et al., 2023 and Gui et al., 2023.

claim: Distinct head and neck cancer subsites are known to have different aetiologies.
source: This is relevant because distinct HNC subsites are known to have different aetiologies (Thomas et al., 2018), although we did not find evidence of heterogeneity across subsites in our analyses investigating the genetically predicted effects of BMI, WHR, and waist circumference on HNC risk.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 2018.

claim: The study did not find evidence of heterogeneity across subsites in analyses investigating the genetically predicted effects of BMI, WHR, and waist circumference on head and neck cancer risk.
source: This is relevant because distinct HNC subsites are known to have different aetiologies (Thomas et al., 2018), although we did not find evidence of heterogeneity across subsites in our analyses investigating the genetically predicted effects of BMI, WHR, and waist circumference on HNC risk.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript text.

claim: The study was limited to individuals of European ancestry.
source: Our study was limited to individuals of European ancestry, so our findings should be replicated in other ancestry groups before being generalised to non-European populations.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript text.

claim: The findings should be replicated in other ancestry groups before being generalised to non-European populations.
source: Our study was limited to individuals of European ancestry, so our findings should be replicated in other ancestry groups before being generalised to non-European populations.
evidence: The claim represents a recommendation based on the study's limitations.

claim: Adiposity does not play a major role in head and neck cancer risk.
source: In conclusion, this study indicates that adiposity does not play a major role in HNC risk.
evidence: The claim is supported by the overall findings of the study.

claim: Obesity is an established risk factor for multiple cancers and other chronic diseases.
source: Although we did not find strong evidence of a causal effect of adiposity on HNC, obesity is an established risk factor for multiple cancers and other chronic diseases (Larsson and Burgess, 2021; Lauby-Secretan et al., 2016; Mariosa et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Larsson and Burgess, 2021; Lauby-Secretan et al., 2016; Mariosa et al., 2019.

claim: There is value in aiming to reduce the levels of excess adiposity in the population.
source: Hence, there is still value in aiming to reduce the levels of excess adiposity in the population.
evidence: The claim represents a recommendation based on established knowledge about obesity as a risk factor for other diseases.
